          file.exists(file.path(post,"figures","rent_burden.html")))

n_increase <- sum(d$change_pp>0)

**Which states saw the largest increase in the share of rent-burdened households between 2019 and 2024?** Comparing housing costs with household income helps identify where a larger share of renter households faced high housing costs relative to their budgets over those five years.

## Measure the pressure on household budgets

I use the Census Bureau’s **ACS 1-year estimates**, [table B25070](https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs1/groups/B25070.html), to compare the same 50 states in 2019 and 2024. Each point represents one state, regardless of its renter population. DC and Puerto Rico are excluded. The two years describe different groups of renter households, so the comparison tracks state shares rather than individual households.

The [Census Bureau’s housing report](https://www2.census.gov/library/publications/2025/demo/acs-61.pdf) describes HUD’s common cost-burden benchmark as spending more than 30% of income on housing. Here, I use **at least 30% of household income on rent and utilities**, as the first included Census category is 30.0-34.9%. This is a comparison threshold, not a universal test of affordability.

Gross rent includes contract rent plus tenant-paid utilities and fuels. The income measure is household income before taxes. I add the four categories from 30% upward and divide by renter households with a computed rent-to-income ratio. The [Census definitions](https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2024_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf) exclude no-rent households and those reporting zero or negative income from that computable group. Consequently, the percentages do **not** cover every renter household.

This percentage shows how common rent burden is. For example, a value of 50% means that half of the renter households included in this calculation spend at least 30% of their income on rent and utilities.

## Comparing increases with 2024 burden levels

The chart starts with the ten largest estimated increases. Each row represents a state, and each point shows the change in percentage points. Horizontal lines show approximate 90% intervals; intervals crossing zero do not clearly distinguish an increase from a decrease.

Select a region to compare its states, or choose **All matching states** to see the full selected group. Hover for the two annual shares and the estimated change. Then switch to **2024 burden share** to check whether a state with a large increase also had a high burden share in 2024. This separates where burdens rose most from where they were highest.

## Where burdens increased most

**Nevada, Maine and Florida** have the **largest estimated increases**: `r f1(v("NV","change_pp"))`, `r f1(v("ME","change_pp"))` and `r f1(v("FL","change_pp"))` percentage points, respectively. Arizona and Nebraska complete the top five, which span all four Census regions.

Nevada’s estimated burden share rises from **`r f1(v("NV","share_2019"))`% to `r f1(v("NV","share_2024"))`%**. However, switching to **2024 burden share** puts Florida first at **`r f1(v("FL","share_2024"))`%**. Nevada therefore has the largest estimated increase, while Florida had the highest estimated burden share in 2024. The two rankings answer different questions. These are estimated rankings; the chart’s intervals show uncertainty in each state’s change.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Top five estimated increases

```{r}
tab <- data.frame(State=top$state,`2019 (%)`=f1(top$share_2019),`2024 (%)`=f1(top$share_2024),
                  `Change (pp)`=f1(top$change_pp),
                  `Approx. 90% change interval (pp)`=paste0("[",f1(top$change_low90),", ",f1(top$change_high90),"]"),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab)
```

:::

## Takeaway

Nevada, Maine and Florida had the largest estimated increases in rent-burden shares between 2019 and 2024: 6.5, 6.3 and 6.2 percentage points. These estimates indicate that a larger share of renter households with a computed rent-to-income ratio spent at least 30% of their income on rent and utilities in 2024 than in 2019.
